hero.headline: Master IELTS Academic Listening
hero.subheadline: Practice with 52 authentic Cambridge-calibrated mock tests, master audio distractors across British, Australian, and North American accents, and train under real examination conditions.

formatRules.summary: The IELTS Listening test evaluates your ability to understand spoken English across both everyday social situations and rigorous academic lectures. It is identical for both IELTS Academic and IELTS Academic candidates.

cards.title: Structure & Progression
points: 4 recorded sections, each containing 10 questions in progressive order of difficulty.
Section 1 starts with everyday social conversation; Section 4 culminates in a specialized university lecture.
You are tested on main ideas, specific factual details, speaker opinions, and purpose.

cards.title: Timing & Playback Rule
points: The audio recording is played ONLY ONCE. You cannot rewind, replay, or pause.
Approximately 30 minutes of continuous audio recording playback.
Paper-based test: You get 10 minutes at the end to transfer answers to the official answer sheet.
Computer-delivered test: You enter answers directly on screen and get 2 minutes to review.

cards.title: Accents & Pronunciation
points: Reflects international English: British, Australian, New Zealand, American, and Canadian accents.
Section 1 frequently features British and Australian native speakers.
Familiarize yourself with varying vowel lengths, elision, and linked speech patterns.

cards.title: Strict Answering Rules
points: Strict word count limits: 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER'. Exceeding this limit results in zero marks.
Both UK and US spelling conventions are accepted (e.g., colour/color, theatre/theater).
Hyphenated words (e.g., part-time) count as a single word. Numbers can be written as figures (14) or words (fourteen).

fourSections.title: Section 1: Everyday Social Dialogue
fourSections.context: Everyday social or transactional context — hotel bookings, leisure club sign-ups, customer service enquiries, renting accommodation.
fourSections.description: A conversation between two people in an everyday social setting. One speaker usually asks questions to extract specific factual details from the other.
fourSections.keyFocus: Names, phone numbers, postcodes, calendar dates, prices, addresses, and flight or booking reference codes.
fourSections.expertTip: Listen attentively to letter-by-letter spelling. Speakers frequently correct themselves mid-dialogue (e.g., 'Oh wait, that is 14 Hill Street, not 40'). Always write the final confirmed detail.

fourSections.title: Section 2: Everyday Social Monologue
fourSections.context: Everyday social situation with a single speaker providing public information — guided museum tour, botanical garden walk, charity event briefing, radio broadcast.
fourSections.description: A monologue set in an everyday social context where one speaker addresses an audience or provides structured guidance on facilities or itineraries.
fourSections.keyFocus: Spatial orientation (north, south, opposite, adjoining), sequential event schedules, amenities, and visitor guidelines.
fourSections.expertTip: For map and plan questions, locate the starting point immediately ('You are here'). Trace the speaker's directional cues using compass bearings and positional prepositions ('turn left past the duck pond').

fourSections.title: Section 3: Academic Discussion
fourSections.context: Academic or educational setting — two university students planning a research presentation, a dissertation student consulting their professor, a seminar study group.
fourSections.description: A discussion involving 2 to 4 people exploring academic coursework, research methodology, scientific experiment design, or seminar paper evaluations.
fourSections.keyFocus: Tracking who says what, subtle nuances of agreement or polite disagreement, shifting hypotheses, and critical evaluations.
fourSections.expertTip: Identify each speaker's voice in the initial 15 seconds. Beware of distractors where one student proposes an idea but the professor or study partner subsequently rejects or refines it.

fourSections.title: Section 4: Academic Monologue / Lecture
fourSections.context: A university lecture or academic presentation on a specialized topic — marine biology, anthropology, urban architecture, renewable energy, ancient archaeology.
fourSections.description: An authentic academic monologue delivering detailed research findings, historical chronologies, or technical explanations without conversational interruptions.
fourSections.keyFocus: Discourse markers ('turning now to', 'more importantly', 'the primary drawback'), dense academic vocabulary, cause-and-effect relationships.
fourSections.expertTip: There is NO pause midway through Section 4. Read all 10 questions during the preparation time. Use the headings and sub-bullets in the notes to stay synchronized with the lecturer.

questionTypes.name: Multiple Choice
questionTypes.format: Choose 1 from 3 options (A, B, C) or 2 from 5 options (A–E)
questionTypes.description: Evaluates your ability to understand specific points or the overall gist of an audio passage while eliminating plausible distractors.
questionTypes.howItWorks: A question stem is followed by three options, or an incomplete sentence with three endings. In multiple-answer tasks, you select two or three correct options from a longer list.
questionTypes.strategy: Underline keywords in the question stem during preparation time. Listen for synonyms and paraphrases rather than exact words. Avoid choosing an option just because a word from it was mentioned; check if the meaning matches.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Selecting an option because you heard an identical word. Test writers deliberately insert words from wrong options as distractors.

questionTypes.name: Matching
questionTypes.format: Match numbered questions (e.g. 21–25) to lettered options (A–G)
questionTypes.description: Assesses your ability to follow a conversation between speakers and link specific items to categories, opinions, or characteristics.
questionTypes.howItWorks: You are given a list of items from the listening text and must match them to a set of criteria or options displayed in a box.
questionTypes.strategy: Focus on the numbered list as your anchor because questions follow the chronological order of the audio. Keep your eyes on the options box to identify the matching concept as you listen.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Losing your place because you spend too much time reading the options list instead of keeping up with the spoken sequence.

questionTypes.name: Plan, Map & Diagram Labelling
questionTypes.format: Complete labels on a map, building floorplan, or mechanical diagram using letters (A–H) or words
questionTypes.description: Tests your spatial awareness and ability to follow spoken directional language, compass bearings, and landmark descriptions.
questionTypes.howItWorks: You are presented with a visual schematic (e.g., a nature park map, library layout, or solar water heater diagram) with numbered blank spaces.
questionTypes.strategy: Find the starting point ('We are standing at the main reception entrance'). Note compass directions (North, South, East, West) and orient yourself to left, right, opposite, adjacent, and circular pathways.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Confusing the speaker's perspective with your own. Always follow the route as the speaker moves through the map.

questionTypes.name: Form Completion
questionTypes.format: Fill in factual blanks on an application form, order form, or registration sheet
questionTypes.description: Tests your precision in recording factual details such as names, contact numbers, dates, times, currency amounts, and reference codes.
questionTypes.howItWorks: An authentic form layout is provided with specific field gaps (e.g. 'Customer Surname', 'Contact Phone', 'Membership Tier').
questionTypes.strategy: Read the field titles carefully. Predict the grammatical category and data type (e.g., number, date, postcode). Practice English alphabet spelling conventions and double letters.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Missing corrections. When a speaker says 'Sorry, that is double L, not single L', make sure you write the amended spelling.

questionTypes.name: Note Completion
questionTypes.format: Fill in gaps in a structured outline, bulleted notes, or lecture summary
questionTypes.description: Assesses your ability to follow a lecture or presentation and record key concepts and supporting evidence within strict word limits.
questionTypes.howItWorks: A hierarchical set of notes with main headings and bulleted sub-points is presented with numbered blanks.
questionTypes.strategy: Use the headings and bold text as signposts to track the speaker's progress. If you miss an answer, move immediately to the next bullet point.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Writing extra words that exceed the instructions (e.g., writing 'in the ancient forest' when the limit is 'NO MORE THAN ONE WORD').

questionTypes.name: Table Completion
questionTypes.format: Complete empty cells inside a structured data table with rows and columns
questionTypes.description: Evaluates your ability to locate and summarize specific categories of information such as dates, costs, locations, or requirements.
questionTypes.howItWorks: A grid or matrix categorizes information into clearly labeled columns (e.g., 'Activity', 'Equipment Provided', 'Cost per Session').
questionTypes.strategy: Scan the column headings from left to right. Understand how rows represent individual cases. Look at completed adjacent cells to deduce the required format.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Misreading row or column intersections and writing the answer in the wrong blank number.

questionTypes.name: Flow-Chart Completion
questionTypes.format: Fill in sequential stages of a process or project timeline with arrows
questionTypes.description: Tests your understanding of chronological stages, procedural steps, cause-and-effect chains, or scientific experiments.
questionTypes.howItWorks: A diagram with boxes connected by directional arrows outlines a sequential process with gaps in specific stages.
questionTypes.strategy: Listen for sequence discourse markers: 'initially', 'the next phase involves', 'subsequently', 'prior to this', 'the final outcome'.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Skipping ahead or falling behind because arrows loop or branch into two concurrent stages.

questionTypes.name: Sentence Completion
questionTypes.format: Fill in missing words within grammatically complete sentences
questionTypes.description: Tests your comprehension of key factual relationships and ability to identify exact words from the audio that complete a written statement.
questionTypes.howItWorks: You read sentences that summarize information from the listening text and insert words directly from what you heard.
questionTypes.strategy: Check the grammar of the sentence before and after inserting your word. The resulting sentence must be grammatically sound and preserve the original meaning.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Changing the form of the word heard in the recording. You should generally use the EXACT word you heard without changing its tense or form.

questionTypes.name: Short-Answer Questions
questionTypes.format: Answer factual questions using 1 to 3 words and/or a number
questionTypes.description: Measures your ability to locate and extract precise factual information such as prices, dimensions, species, or reasons.
questionTypes.howItWorks: You are asked direct questions (e.g. 'What two items must students bring to the fieldwork?').
questionTypes.strategy: Identify the question word (What, Who, Where, When, Why, How many). Keep your answer strictly within the specified word count.
questionTypes.commonPitfall: Writing full sentence answers instead of concise note-style answers (e.g., writing 'Students need to bring rubber boots' instead of 'rubber boots').

scoringTable.desc: Fluent, accurate comprehension of complex native speech including nuanced academic argumentation.
Handles complex, detailed debate with only occasional unsystematic misunderstandings.
Full operational command; understands detailed academic monologues and rapid multi-speaker dialogue.
Solid operational grasp; handles complex language well and comprehends detailed reasoning in most contexts.
Generally handles complex language well; understands detailed instructions with minor lapses under pressure.
Effective command despite inaccuracies; grasps main ideas and specific factual details in familiar contexts.
Adequate command; understands straightforward factual English but may struggle with rapid colloquialisms or dense theory.
Partial command; copes with overall meaning in common situations but makes frequent errors with fine details.
Partial command; likely to misunderstand abstract discussions or multi-part complex directions.
Basic understanding limited to familiar social contexts; frequent breakdowns in comprehension.
Basic competence is limited; unable to understand complex sentence structures or fast native delivery.
Conveys and understands only isolated words in highly structured situations.

items.title: Underline Anchor Keywords
items.desc: Before audio begins, underline unchangeable words like proper names, dates, technical terms, and place names that cannot easily be paraphrased.

items.title: Predict Word Grammatical Category
items.desc: Analyze the gap: does it require a noun, an adjective, a plural noun, a verb in past tense, or a numerical price? Knowing this primes your auditory cortex.

items.title: Verify Singular vs Plural Requirements
items.desc: Check the surrounding syntax: if the text says 'a variety of _____', it will almost certainly be a plural noun or an uncountable noun.

items.title: Beware the 'Correction Trap'
items.desc: Speakers routinely say one thing and immediately correct themselves: 'We planned to open on Tuesday, but due to refurbishments it has been postponed to Friday.' The answer is Friday.

items.title: Map Synonyms & Paraphrasing in Real Time
items.desc: The question might say 'inexpensive accommodation' while the recording says 'budget-friendly lodgings' or 'low-cost rooms'. Never wait for identical words.

items.title: Track Discourse Signpost Markers
items.desc: Words like 'however', 'conversely', 'the crucial point', 'turning now to' signal major structural shifts in the speaker's argument or the next answer.

items.title: Keep Moving — Never Freeze on a Missed Blank
items.desc: If you realize you missed Question 14, immediately let it go and look ahead to Question 15. Hesitating on one missed blank can cause you to miss 3 more.

items.title: Strictly Check Word Count Limits
items.desc: If the instruction states 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS', writing 'in the green forest' (4 words) gives you zero marks even if the meaning is correct. Write 'green forest'.

items.title: Scrutinize Spelling & Capitalization
items.desc: Misspelled words are marked completely wrong. Common pitfalls: necessary, accommodate, environment, government, separate, restaurant, recommendation.

items.title: Ensure No Blank Spaces on Answer Sheet
items.desc: There is NO negative marking in IELTS Listening. Never leave an empty box; make an educated guess based on context if needed.

interactiveDrills.title: Mini-Drill 1: Hotel Conference Booking (Section 1 Form)
interactiveDrills.instruction: Listen to the simulated audio excerpt and complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
interactiveDrills.audioTranscript:
Receptionist: Good morning, Grand Royale Executive Suites, how may I direct your call?
Caller: Hello, I'm calling to confirm our department conference booking for next month. It's under the name Harrison, that's Marcus Harrison.
Receptionist: Yes Mr. Harrison, I have the booking here. You requested the Cedar Suite for the 18th of October.
Caller: That's right. Could we update the delegate count to 45 attendees? We originally thought 40, but five additional regional directors are joining.
Receptionist: Certainly, 45 delegates noted. And regarding the luncheon menu, did you prefer the hot buffet or the cold deli platters?
Caller: Actually, we decided on the Mediterranean buffet. Most of our delegates prefer vegetarian options.
Receptionist: Excellent. And I have your primary contact number as 07952 481903, correct?
Caller: Ah, that's my old office desk phone. Could you update that to my direct mobile? It is 07952 642318.
Receptionist: All updated, Mr. Harrison. We will email the confirmation summary to you this afternoon.

questions.label: 1. Conference Suite Name:
questions.explanation: The receptionist confirms the room as the 'Cedar Suite'.

questions.label: 2. Final number of delegates:
questions.explanation: They originally planned 40, but added 5 regional directors, bringing the confirmed total to 45.

questions.label: 3. Selected Luncheon Option:
questions.explanation: The caller specifically opts for the 'Mediterranean buffet' to accommodate dietary preferences.

questions.label: 4. Direct Mobile Contact:
questions.explanation: The caller replaces the old office phone with direct mobile number 07952 642318.

interactiveDrills.title: Mini-Drill 2: Marine Biology Seminar (Section 3 Distractor Trap)
interactiveDrills.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, or C.
interactiveDrills.audioTranscript:
Professor: Now Liam, before we review your coral reef survey data, what did you decide regarding the water depth parameters?
Liam: Well, our supervisor initially suggested taking samples down at 25 metres where human disturbance is minimal. And Chloe thought 10 metres would give us the richest biodiversity.
Professor: Both valid points. But what did your team actually do?
Liam: After checking the tidal currents on the reef crest, we concluded that 15 metres was the only depth where our sensor equipment could maintain steady calibration for the full 48-hour cycle.
Professor: That makes complete methodological sense.

question.text: At what depth did the research team take their continuous sensor samples?

options.text: 15 metres (due to sensor calibration and currents)

question.explanation: 10 metres was Chloe's idea, and 25 metres was the supervisor's recommendation (both distractors). The team actually decided on 15 metres due to tidal currents and sensor stability.

faqs.q: How many questions are there in IELTS Listening and how long does it take?
faqs.a: The IELTS Listening examination consists of 40 questions split across 4 sections (10 questions per section). The audio recording plays for approximately 30 minutes without pauses. In the paper-based exam, you get 10 minutes at the end to transfer your handwritten notes to the official answer sheet. In the computer-delivered exam, you get 2 minutes to review your answers on screen.

faqs.q: Can I listen to the audio recording more than once?
faqs.a: No. The recording is played strictly ONCE. There are no replays or pauses. This is why previewing questions during the allocated 30–45 second preparation intervals before each section and underlining keywords is critical to anticipating answers before they are spoken.

faqs.q: Are the Listening questions identical for Academic and Academic?
faqs.a: Yes. Unlike the Reading and Writing modules which differ between Academic and Academic, the IELTS Listening test is completely identical for both candidate groups. Both groups face the exact same recording, question types, and scoring conversion curve.

faqs.q: What happens if I write more words than the specified word limit?
faqs.a: If an instruction says 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS' and you write three words, your answer is automatically marked incorrect and receives zero marks, even if the correct keyword was part of your phrase. Always check the word limit instruction at the beginning of every question set.

faqs.q: Is spelling strictly checked in IELTS Listening?
faqs.a: Yes, spelling accuracy is absolute. If a word is misspelled (for example, writing 'enviroment' instead of 'environment' or 'accomodation' instead of 'accommodation'), you lose the mark. Both standard British English and American English spellings are accepted (e.g., color or colour, centre or center).

faqs.q: Are hyphenated words and numbers counted as one word?
faqs.a: Yes. Hyphenated words such as 'part-time' or 'well-known' count as a single word. Numbers can be written as numerals (e.g., 25) or as words (e.g., twenty-five), and either counts as a single number/word.

faqs.q: What accents will I hear on the test?
faqs.a: The IELTS test is an international English test. You will hear authentic native speakers with British, Australian, New Zealand, American, and Canadian accents. Practicing with a wide variety of English media and dialect podcasts ensures you are not caught off guard by regional vowel shifts or colloquial pacing.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss an answer while listening?
faqs.a: Never panic or stop listening. The recording will continue moving forward. If you freeze trying to remember a missed blank, you will likely miss the subsequent 2 or 3 questions as well. Immediately skip the missed item, focus your attention on the keywords of the next question, and make an educated guess on the missed blank during the final transfer/review window.
